title: The sun's gift in the forest
hookLine: the Brahmanas follow the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira has nothing to feed them until the sun gives a vessel
carry: surya: the sun who ripens food for all
tomorrow: Where was Krishna during the game?

lines: HOW DO YOU FEED THOSE WHO STAY?
cards: A crowd is following the exiles. The Pandavas have lost their kingdom, their wealth and their palace, and still a company of Brahmanas keeps walking behind them into the trees, refusing to turn back.
That night, by the water, Yudhishthira lies awake with a very practical problem. He can't send his guests away; a host doesn't do that. And he has nothing to feed them.
How do you feed the people who chose to stay?

teach.b: The family priest, Dhaumya, gives him counsel. Turn to Surya, the sun, he says: it is the sun that ripens what the earth gives, and so feeds every creature.
In Ganguli's telling, Dhaumya teaches him a hundred and eight names of the sun. So Yudhishthira purifies himself with water, and praises the sun.
And Surya appears, blazing, with a gift: a copper vessel.
Whatever is cooked in your kitchen, the sun tells him, won't run out for your guests, as long as Draupadi hasn't yet eaten. So the forest household finds its shape.
Draupadi serves the Brahmanas first, then her husbands, and only after everyone has eaten does she eat, and the vessel is done for the day. Here's the teaching under the story.
Hindus honor the sun as a god, Surya, because every meal starts with him: he ripens the grain.
That's why so many Hindus still greet the morning sun by pouring out a little water toward it, an offering called arghya, often standing in a river.
And at the autumn festival of Chhath, families from Bihar and nearby regions fast, then stand in rivers and lakes at sunset and again at sunrise, offering to the sun in thanks for harvest and life.
When the Pandavas had lost everything, they started by thanking the one who feeds every creature. Their camp didn't get a palace back. It got a table.

how: The story of Surya's vessel is retold in Hindu storytelling, and the sun's place as the giver of food lives on in the daily offering of water, arghya, and in the festival of Chhath.

o: a vow to live on roots and fruit alone
the forest where the Pandavas live out their exile
the hermitage where Vyasa teaches his students

games.q: the forest kitchen — tap the pairs.
p: counsels Yudhishthira to turn to the sun
standing in water to thank the sun

s: the vessel gave food without end, no matter what
it kept giving only until Draupadi had eaten.
Dhaumya told Yudhishthira to turn to the sun
the sun ripens what the earth gives, he said, and so feeds every creature.
offering water to the sun is an old custom no Hindu keeps now
many offer arghya each morning, and families keep Chhath standing in rivers and lakes.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. you've lost everything, and a crowd of Brahmanas has followed you into the forest. you can't feed them. what do you do?
o: send them back to the city.
ask your priest what to do, and turn to the sun.
go back and beg from the Kauravas.
games.why: he takes Dhaumya's counsel, praises Surya, the sun who ripens food for all, and receives a vessel whose food lasts until Draupadi eats.

practice: Hold a glass of water, or picture one, and face the brightest window you have. Many Hindus offer water toward the morning sun, arghya, with a simple line like om suryaya namah.
If you pray, say it and give thanks for the food today will bring; if you don't, pour the water on a plant tomorrow and think of the sun inside your next meal.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest of exile, where the Pandavas keep a table with almost nothing but a vessel from the sun.

orig.note: Sanskrit arghya: water offered in honor, as many Hindus pour it toward the morning sun.

carryVoice: Your line: surya: the sun who ripens food for all. In the forest, his gift fed every guest first. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), early sections (the Brahmanas follow; Dhaumya's counsel; Yudhishthira praises Surya; the copper vessel)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva, sec. 3 in Ganguli (Dhaumya teaches Yudhishthira the hundred and eight names of Surya)
Living practice: arghya, water offered to the sun at dawn; Chhath Puja (Bihar, Jharkhand, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Nepal's Terai), offerings to the setting and rising sun while standing in water
